fixes.explanation: Close, friend, but that's a different cave. David escaped to the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), and he later became king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). Here the five kings hide at Makkedah. Lots of caves in this land, so it's easy to mix them up.

Nice try, baker, but no trench in this passage. The text has Joshua order large stones rolled against the mouth of the cave. He also has men posted there to guard it. The cave gets a door made of stones, and that's the whole plan.

Right on target. Joshua tells them, "But you, do not stop there. Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind." The kings are shut in the cave, so the rest of the men keep moving. No standing around by the stones for this crew.

Not yet, baker. Joshua says, "But you, do not stop there." and sends the men after the enemy. The army does come back to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah, but only after the chase is finished (Joshua 10:20-21). The order for now is to keep going.

No boats in this one, baker. The word is cities. Joshua tells his men not to let the enemy reach their cities, because the LORD has delivered them into their hand. Nobody in this passage is heading for the harbor.
That's right. The text says, "…no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites." After the chase, the army is back with Joshua at Makkedah. Nobody dared say a word against them.

Yes, baker. Joshua summons all the men of Israel, then speaks to the army commanders who had come with him. They come forward and put their feet on the necks of the kings (Joshua 10:24). Then Joshua tells them, "Be strong and courageous."

The Gibeonites are the people of Gibeon, the city the five kings had gone to war against (Joshua 10:5). The text doesn't name them in this scene, baker. Joshua tells the army commanders who came with him to put their feet on the kings' necks. Gibeon is where this whole story began, so it's easy to keep them in mind.

That's the one, baker. The text says the stones are there "…to this day." The writer tells us the stones were still at the mouth of that cave when it was written. At sunset the bodies were thrown into the cave, and then large stones were placed against its mouth.

Yes, baker. The text says Joshua did this "…just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded." This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's okay to feel that. The text tells us who gave the command: the LORD, the God of Israel.

The text doesn't give that as the reason, baker. It does say the survivors retreated to the fortified cities (Joshua 10:20). The reason it gives for the win is that "…the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel…" That's the answer on the page.
That's right. The passage ends with, "Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal." The campaign is done, and Joshua brings all Israel back to camp. That's where this chapter closes.
